children: 1341 ET - Home sales in California hit their lowest level in nearly three-years in October, the California Association of Realtors says. Closed escrow sales of existing, single-family detached homes in California reached a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 246,830 in October, the Association says. This was down from 260,410 in September, and 12.7% percent lower from October of last year. Statewide, sales remained below the 300,000-unit benchmark for the 49th consecutive month, the Association adds. "When mortgage rates jumped to a nearly three-year high in late September, we saw many buyers step back and reassess what they could afford, which led to fewer closed sales in October," says Mark Peterson, 2027 president of the Association. The statewide median home price fell to $886,760 in October from $899,720 in September. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1211 ET - General Motors is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Chief Executive Mary Barra, The Wall Street Journal reported. The automaker is also eyeing a crop of internal candidates, according to people familiar with the matter. Barra has led GM since 2014, making her the company's second-longest tenured CEO. (kelly.cloonan@wsj.com)

1141 ET - Viking CEO Leah Talactac says the historically low water levels that hurt portions of the cruise operator's river operations were an anomaly and that conditions are beginning to improve. Some fluctuation in water level is typical, Talactac says on a call with analysts. "2026 was unique due to the unprecedented combination of duration, severity and geographic breadth," she continues. "Multiple sections of the Rhine, Main and Danube rivers were affected simultaneously and remained impacted for an extended period." Water-level trends are anticipated to improve throughout the remainder of the year, though, thanks to recent rainfall and current forecasts for additional precipitation in the coming days, Talactac says. (connor.hart@wsj.com)

1138 ET - Viking says historically low water levels hurt portions of its European river operations during the recent quarter. The cruise company says the low-water disruptions reduced 3Q revenue and adjusted gross margin each by about $100 million, reflecting guest cancellations and incremental costs tied to mitigation efforts. "As we have done in prior disruptions, we leveraged our experience, scale and operational flexibility to minimize the impact on our guests," CEO Leah Talactac says on a call with analysts. "Drawing on nearly 30 years of river cruising experience and the flexibility of our identical fleet of long ships, we operated all scheduled voyages through ship swaps, itinerary modifications, alternative transportation and additional accommodations where needed." (connor.hart@wsj.com)

1115 ET - Treasury yields and the dollar lose steam and fall following an unexpected drop in the November NAHB Housing Market Index. Confidence among U.S. home builders drops to its lowest level since April 2012 amid elevated costs and high mortgage rates. Industrial production falls in October, also surprising on the downside. Bond markets change direction after the data and the 10-year trades at 5.107%, down from 5.151% earlier. The WSJ Dollar Index falls slightly, as the dollar weakens 0.1% against the yen and the euro. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1032 ET - Investor Steve Eisman says AI neocloud companies are in a tough spot after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company after an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and another alleged affair with a senior executive at Nvidia. Huang "created what I call a virtual, vertical holding company, and it's unwinding," he says during an appearance on CNBC. Eisman says that while no one knows exactly what the ramifications will be, "the neoclouds are all in big trouble," given data center construction is so closely tied to Nvidia. Eisman is a money manager who successfully bet against the subprime mortgage craze ahead of the 2008-09 financial crisis.   (kelly.cloonan@wsj.com)

1011 ET - Amazon launches its own line of ready-to-eat and heat-and-eat meals. Jason Buechel, VP of Amazon Worldwide Grocery Stores, says "Customers want delicious, high-quality meals that fit into their lives, without the hassle of cooking or the cost of takeout." He adds that customers can add a ready-made meal "to the same cart as millions of other items they shop for on Amazon and have it delivered the same day." The new line includes breakfast offerings, salads and soups for lunch, and dinner entrées--all of which are priced under $8, the company says. The launch comes as Amazon has worked to grow its online grocery business and expand its Whole Foods Market business in recent years. (connor.hart@wsj.com)

1007 ET - Klarna says its customers are using its services for more of their everyday purchases as well as larger-ticket items. Categories like events and services and home and electronics took up a bigger share of the buy now, pay later company's overall gross merchandise volume--which measures the total monetary value of all completed purchases over its network--in the latest quarter. Apparel and accessories purchases took up a smaller share as the network continues to diversify, the company says. (kelly.cloonan@wsj.com)

0954 ET - UBS analysts are bullish on the near-term set up for U.S. airlines, saying the combination of lower jet fuel costs and resilient demand creates an increasingly favorable setup. "Gulf Coast jet fuel is down 18% over the past month while our checks suggest demand remains strong and the industry continues to push through select price increases," the analysts say in a research note. "Against this backdrop, we see upside to 4Q EPS for most airlines, despite the drag from this weekend's FAA-mandated ground stop." More importantly, they add, the analysts move their 2027 estimates meaningfully higher. UBS favors Allegiant, Southwest, Alaska and American in the near term, while picking Delta and United over the long term. (connor.hart@wsj.com)

0910 ET - Disney expects to deliver $3 billion in annual cost savings by fiscal 2029--cuts that come as new CEO Josh D'Amaro works to transform the entertainment company to better compete in the global streaming market. As part of its effort, Disney has cut thousands of jobs this year in several rounds of layoffs, along with a voluntary exit program for long-tenured employees. "Changes like these are not easy, and they affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company," D'Amaro says on a call with analysts. "At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth." Disney slips 2.5% premarket. (connor.hart@wsj.com)

0859 ET - Disney will concentrate its investments in what CEO Josh D'Amaro calls the company's two biggest growth areas: streaming and experiences. "In streaming, we intend to bring more of our world-class entertainment and sports content to a growing fan base around the world," he says on a call with analysts. Disney says it will increase its content spending in the coming fiscal year. At the same time, the company is working to increase capacity across its theme parks and cruises, with new projects currently underway across both portfolios, D'Amaro says. "Of course, technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," he says. "Our product teams have made meaningful improvements to the Disney+ user experience, and we're seeing the impact in our financial results." (connor.hart@wsj.com)

0855 ET - Treasury yields gain momentum as October retail sales surprise on the upside. While overall sales meet expectations and rise 0.2%, sales ex-auto come in at 0.6%, versus WSJ consensus of 0.4%. The readings are softer than in September. Import prices rise more than expected, at 1.1%. The data keep the Fed on track for a hike in December. Wall Street also looks at Nvidia's earnings and guidance after the close. The DXY dollar index rises to a 19-month high, while crude oil is up 1%. The 10-year yield is at 5.137%, up from 5.122% yesterday. The two-year rises to 4.851% from 4.825%. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)
